extracted.subtask_description: A set of eight Standards for Mathematical Practice describing the habits of mind and proficiencies mathematics educators should develop in students, grounded in NCTM process standards and NRC strands of mathematical proficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundations: NCTM process standards and NRC proficiency strands
rubrics_metrics.description: The Standards for Mathematical Practice rest on important 'processes and proficiencies' with longstanding importance: the NCTM process standards of problem solving, reasoning and proof, communication, representation, and connections; and the NRC's strands of mathematical proficiency: adaptive reasoning, strategic competence, conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, and productive disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NRC strands are further characterized: conceptual understanding (comprehension of mathematical concepts, operations and relations), procedural fluency (skill in carrying out procedures flexibly, accurately, efficiently and appropriately), and productive disposition (habitual inclination to see mathematics as sensible, useful, and worthwhile, coupled with a belief in diligence and one’s own efficacy). These frameworks provide the background for the eight specific practice standards that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution; they analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution, consider analogous problems, try special cases and simpler forms, monitor and evaluate progress, and change course if necessary. Examples: older students may transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on a graphing calculator; younger students might use concrete objects or pictures. Students check answers using a different method and continually ask 'Does this make sense?' They can understand others' approaches and identify correspondences between different approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason abstractly and quantitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Students make sense of quantities and their relationships by both decontextualizing (abstracting and representing symbolically) and contextualizing (pausing to consider referents during manipulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative reasoning involves creating coherent representations of problems, considering units, attending to the meaning of quantities (not just computations), and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Students understand and use assumptions, definitions, and prior results to construct arguments, make conjectures, and build logical progressions to explore truth, and they can analyze, justify, and communicate conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They analyze situations by breaking into cases, recognize and use counterexamples, reason inductively about data, compare effectiveness of plausible arguments, distinguish correct from flawed reasoning, and explain flaws. Elementary students can argue using concrete referents (objects, drawings, diagrams, actions); later students determine domains of applicability. Students at all grades should listen/read others' arguments, decide if they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model with mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Students apply mathematics to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace by identifying important quantities, mapping relationships, and analyzing those relationships mathematically to draw and interpret conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early grades: write simple equations to describe situations; middle grades: use proportional reasoning for real tasks; high school: use geometry or functions for design/relationships. Proficient modelers make assumptions and approximations to simplify complex situations (and revise them as needed), use tools such as diagrams, tables, graphs, flowcharts, and formulas, interpret results in context, and improve models if they do not serve their purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate tools strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Students consider available tools (pencil and paper, concrete models, ruler, protractor, calculator, spreadsheet, CAS, statistical packages, dynamic geometry software, etc.) and decide when each might be helpful, recognizing both insights gained and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be sufficiently familiar with grade-appropriate tools to make sound decisions. Examples: high school students analyze graphs and solutions generated by graphing calculators and detect possible errors using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. Technology can help visualize varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Students should also identify and use relevant external mathematical resources (e.g., digital content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Students try to communicate precisely, using clear definitions, stating meanings of chosen symbols, and using symbols (including the equal sign) consistently and appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They specify units of measure and label axes to clarify correspondences with problem quantities, calculate accurately and efficiently, and express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate to context. Elementary students give carefully formulated explanations to each other; by high school, students examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for and make use of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Students look closely to discern patterns or structure and use those to simplify or solve problems (e.g., recognizing commutativity or distributive patterns, factoring structure in expressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: young students notice 3 + 7 = 7 + 3 or sort shapes by sides; later students see 7×8 as 7×5 + 7×3 in preparation for the distributive property, or recognize factors in x^2 + 9x + 14. They can use geometric lines (auxiliary lines) and shift perspective to see complicated things as single objects or compositions, using that understanding to bound or analyze expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Students notice when calculations repeat and seek general methods or shortcuts, using repeated observations to abstract general formulas or patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: recognizing a repeating decimal when dividing 25 by 11; abstracting (y–2)/(x–1)=3 from repeated slope checks; noticing cancellation patterns in products that lead to geometric series formulas. While solving, students maintain oversight of the process, attend to details, and continually evaluate the reasonableness of intermediate results.
